question: Among the Linux kernel features that make containers possible, which of the following correctly pairs namespaces and cgroups (control groups) with their roles?
choices: Namespaces: separate what a process can see (process IDs, network, mounts, etc.); cgroups: limit and account for the use of resources such as CPU and memory
Namespaces: limit and account for the use of resources such as CPU and memory; cgroups: separate what a process can see (process IDs, network, mounts, etc.)
Namespaces: boot a separate kernel for each container to isolate them; cgroups: create a virtual CPU for each container and emulate the hardware
explanation: A container is an ordinary process running on the host kernel, isolated by two mechanisms. Namespaces split process IDs, the network, mounts (the view of the file system), the host name and so on into groups, so that the processes in a container see only their own share. Cgroups limit the CPU time and amount of memory a group of processes can use and account for their usage. Both are kernel features, so a container neither boots another kernel nor emulates hardware.
choiceNotes: Correct. Namespaces handle "what is visible" and cgroups handle "how much can be used".
The roles are swapped. Cgroups limit the amount of resources, and namespaces separate the view.
Running a separate kernel or emulating hardware is how virtual machines on a hypervisor work. Containers share the host kernel.

question: On a Linux host, Docker is used to start a container from an image based on a different distribution from the host, and uname -r (which shows the kernel release) and cat /etc/os-release (which shows information about the distribution) are run inside it. Which of the following correctly describes the results?
choices: Both uname -r and /etc/os-release show information about the host kernel and the host distribution
Both uname -r and /etc/os-release show information about the distribution the image is based on and its kernel
uname -r shows the host kernel, and /etc/os-release shows the distribution of the image
explanation: A container shares the host kernel, so uname -r, which asks the kernel, shows the release of the host kernel even inside the container. /etc/os-release, on the other hand, is a file, so it is read from the file system the container sees, that is, from the image, and it shows the name of the image's distribution. An image contains no kernel, only user-space files such as commands and libraries. For this reason, a program that relies on a feature the host kernel lacks will not work inside a container either.
choiceNotes: /etc/os-release is a file in the container's file system, so the contents of the image are read.
An image contains no kernel. The host kernel is shared, so uname -r shows the host release.
Correct. The kernel is shared with the host, while the files seen are those of the image.

question: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between a container image and a container?
choices: When a container is stopped, the changes made inside it are automatically written back to the image, overwriting the original image
An image is a read-only template, and several containers, each with its own writable layer, can be started from one image
Only one container at a time can be started from an image, and starting a second one requires copying the image under another name first
explanation: An image is a read-only template that bundles the files and settings needed to run an application, and a container is a unit of execution created from an image. When a container is created, a writable layer of its own is stacked on top of the image's layers. Many containers can therefore be started from one image, and changes in one container affect neither the other containers nor the image. To keep a change as part of an image, the usual approach is to edit the Dockerfile and rebuild the image.
choiceNotes: Changes made in a container stay only in that container's writable layer; the image does not change automatically.
Correct. The image is shared, and each container gets its own writable layer.
Any number of containers can be started from the same image. There is no need to copy the image.

question: Inside a container started from an image, the configuration file /etc/app.conf, which is part of the image, is modified. Which of the following correctly describes what happens with Docker's usual storage mechanism (such as overlay2)?
choices: The file is copied into the container's writable layer and then modified, so the image and other containers are not affected
The file in the image layer is modified directly, so other containers started from the same image also see the new contents
Image layers are read-only, so files contained in the image cannot be modified, and the write fails with an error
explanation: A container's file system presents the read-only image layers with a writable layer for that container stacked on top, as a single tree. The first time a file in a lower layer is modified, it is copied into the writable layer, and from then on the copy is used (copy-on-write). The image layers therefore stay unchanged, and other containers sharing the same image are not affected. Because the first copy of a large file takes time, data that is written frequently, such as database data, is placed in a volume.
choiceNotes: Correct. On the first write, the file is copied into the writable layer.
Image layers are read-only and shared by several containers, so they are not modified directly.
The write does not fail; it happens after the file is copied into the writable layer.

question: To unpack a 500 MB archive, data.tar.gz, an image was built with the Dockerfile above. Although the archive was deleted in the same RUN after unpacking, the image remained larger by the size of the archive. Which of the following is the most appropriate pair of reason and remedy?
code:
FROM alpine
COPY data.tar.gz /tmp/
RUN tar -xzf /tmp/data.tar.gz -C /opt && rm /tmp/data.tar.gz
choices: The rm after && is not executed during the build. Write the rm as a separate RUN instruction
Deleted files remain in the image as build cache. Build again with --no-cache added to docker build
The archive remains in the layer created by the COPY instruction. Use a multi-stage build and copy only the unpacked files into the final image
explanation: Each Dockerfile instruction that changes the file system (such as COPY or RUN) becomes one layer, and an image is these layers stacked together. Deleting a file in a later layer only records a deletion marker in the upper layer, so the 500 MB archive that went into the COPY layer remains in the image. With a multi-stage build that unpacks in another stage and brings only the unpacked files into the last stage with COPY --from, the archive is not included in the final image. Downloading, unpacking and deleting within one RUN is another approach, but it cannot be used for a file brought in with COPY.
choiceNotes: The rm after && also runs within the same RUN. Moving it to a separate RUN just adds a layer with the deletion marker and does not reduce the size.
--no-cache only stops the results of earlier builds from being reused; the layer contents are the same, so the size does not change.
Correct. The contents of a lower layer remain even after deletion, so keep the archive out of the final image.

question: There are five images, each of which stacks its own 30 MB layer on the same base image (120 MB). Layer compression and the size of metadata are ignored. Which of the following is the disk space used by the images when all five are pulled to one server?
choices: 150 MB
270 MB
750 MB
explanation: Image layers are identified by a digest computed from their contents, and an identical layer is stored only once on a server and shared by several images. The 120 MB base layer is stored once, and the five unique layers take 30 MB × 5 = 150 MB, so the total is 120 + 150 = 270 MB. That is 480 MB less than the 750 MB, (120 + 30) × 5, that would be needed without sharing. Using a common base image reduces pull time and disk usage.
choiceNotes: 120 + 30 = 150 MB is the size of a single image. All five unique layers are needed.
(120 + 30) × 5 = 750 MB is the value if the base layer were not shared.

question: For the Dockerfile above, which of the following correctly pairs the command executed when the image is built with docker build and the command executed when a container is started with docker run?
code:
FROM python:slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
choices: At build: pip install; at run: python app.py
At build: pip install and python app.py; at run: python app.py
At build: nothing; at run: pip install and python app.py
explanation: RUN executes a command while the image is being built and saves the result (here, the installed libraries) in the image as a new layer. CMD only records, as part of the image configuration, the default command to execute when a container starts; it is not executed during the build. The libraries are therefore installed once, at build time, and python app.py runs every time a container starts. If a command is written after the image name in docker run, it replaces the contents of CMD.
choiceNotes: Correct. RUN executes at build time and CMD at start-up.
CMD is not executed during the build. It only records the default command for start-up.
RUN executes during the build and its result is saved in the image. Nothing is reinstalled each time a container starts.

question: An image named pinger, built from the Dockerfile above, is started with docker run pinger example.com. Which of the following is the command executed in the container?
choices: ping -c 3 localhost
ping -c 3 example.com
example.com (an attempt to run it as a command fails with an error)
explanation: An ENTRYPOINT written in exec form (a JSON array) is the command the container always runs, and CMD supplies its default arguments. Arguments written after the image name in docker run replace CMD and are appended after the ENTRYPOINT, so ping -c 3 example.com is executed. Started without arguments as docker run pinger, the localhost in CMD would be used, giving ping -c 3 localhost. To change the ENTRYPOINT itself, use the --entrypoint option of docker run.
choiceNotes: This is what happens when the container is started without arguments. The arguments of docker run replace CMD.
Correct. The argument example.com replaces localhost in CMD and is appended after the ENTRYPOINT.
This would happen with an image that has only CMD and no ENTRYPOINT, because the argument would replace the whole command. Here there is an ENTRYPOINT, so it is passed as an argument.

question: A container is started with the command above from the image nginx, a web server that listens on port 80. The host's IP address is 192.0.2.10, and there are no restrictions such as a firewall. Which of the following is the URL to use to reach this web server from a browser on another PC on the same network?
choices: http://(container IP address):8080/
explanation: The option is written as -p host port:container port, so -p 8080:80 forwards traffic arriving at port 8080 on the host to port 80 in the container. From another PC, connect to port 8080 at the host's IP address. The container's IP address generally belongs to a virtual network inside the host and cannot be reached directly from other PCs. EXPOSE 80 in a Dockerfile only records which port the container uses; it does not publish a host port by itself, so -p is needed.
choiceNotes: Nothing is assigned to port 80 on the host. 80 is the port on the container side.
The container's IP address belongs to a virtual network inside the host and generally cannot be reached from other PCs. Also, the container listens on 80, not 8080.
Correct. The first number is the host port and the second is the container port.

question: Dockerfile (B) above was made from Dockerfile (A), which had RUN npm ci after COPY . ., by changing the order so that only the dependency files are copied first. npm ci takes 120 seconds, npm run build 30 seconds and COPY . . 2 seconds, and the time of the other instructions is negligible. The image is rebuilt 20 times a day after changing only the source code under src (package.json and package-lock.json are unchanged). When the cache from the previous build can be used, which of the following is how much shorter B is than A in total build time per day?
code:
FROM node:lts
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
choices: 2 minutes
About 11 minutes
40 minutes
explanation: The build cache is used instruction by instruction, and for COPY it depends on whether the contents of the copied files are the same as last time. Once the cache cannot be used for an instruction, every instruction after it is executed again. In A, the change is found at the first COPY . ., so every build takes 2 + 120 + 30 = 152 seconds. In B, package.json and package-lock.json are unchanged, so the cache is used up to npm ci, and only COPY . . and npm run build run, taking 2 + 30 = 32 seconds. The difference is 120 seconds per build, or 2,400 seconds = 40 minutes for 20 builds.
choiceNotes: This is the difference for one build (120 seconds = 2 minutes). The image is rebuilt 20 times a day, so multiply by 20.
This is B's daily total (32 seconds × 20 = 640 seconds, about 11 minutes), not the difference from A.
Correct. (152 − 32) × 20 = 2,400 seconds = 40 minutes.

question: In Docker, which of the following correctly describes named volumes and bind mounts, used to keep data written by a container?
choices: A volume is stored in an area managed by Docker and a bind mount in a host directory you specify, and both remain after the container is removed
Data in a named volume remains after the container is removed, but data in a bind mount also disappears from the host directory when the container is removed
Both are created as part of the container's writable layer, so removing the container with docker rm also deletes the data
explanation: Data written to a container's writable layer disappears when the container is removed, so data that must be kept is placed outside the container. A named volume is created in an area managed by Docker and remains until it is explicitly deleted, for example with docker volume rm. A bind mount makes any host directory visible inside the container, and the data simply remains as files on the host. Bind mounts are common during development, when source code edited on the host should take effect immediately, and volumes are common for data whose management is best left to Docker, such as database data.
choiceNotes: Correct. The locations differ, but both are outside the container, so the data remains.
The data of a bind mount is the files in the host directory themselves, so removing the container does not delete them.
Both are outside the container's writable layer, so they remain after the container is removed.

question: An image is pulled by specifying registry.example.com/team/web:1.4. Which of the following correctly gives the meaning of each part of this reference?
choices: registry.example.com: repository; team/web: tag; 1.4: digest computed from the image contents
registry.example.com: registry (the server that stores images); team/web: repository; 1.4: tag
registry.example.com: registry; team: repository; web: tag; 1.4: name of the container to start
explanation: An image reference has the form "registry/repository:tag": the registry is the server that stores and distributes images, the repository groups images of the same kind, and the tag is a name for a version or the like; in this example, registry.example.com is the registry, team/web the repository and 1.4 the tag. If the registry is omitted, the default registry (Docker Hub) is used, and if the tag is omitted, latest is used. A tag is a name given by users, and the same tag can later be moved to a different image. The identifier that always changes when the contents change is the digest beginning with sha256, which is specified after @.
choiceNotes: 1.4 is a tag given by users. A digest is specified in the form "@sha256:…".
Correct. The registry, repository and tag appear in that order.
The whole of team/web is the repository name, and 1.4 is the tag. A container name is given at docker run.

question: scratch is an empty image that contains no files. Which of the following correctly describes what the final image built with the multi-stage Dockerfile above contains?
code:
FROM golang AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/app .

FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
choices: Only the executable /app built in the build stage; the Go compiler and the source code are not included
The layers of the build stage and the last stage are all stacked, so the Go compiler, the source code and /app are all included
Only the golang image of the first FROM and the source code; /app is built each time a container starts
explanation: In a multi-stage build, each FROM starts a stage, and only the last stage becomes the final image. Earlier stages exist to produce artifacts with tools such as compilers, and only the files named in COPY --from are brought into the last stage. Here only /app is copied onto the empty scratch image, so the result is a small image without the Go compiler or the source code. Because scratch has no shared libraries either, CGO_ENABLED=0 is used to build an executable that does not depend on other libraries. Fewer contents mean faster pulls and fewer tools for attackers and fewer targets for vulnerabilities.
choiceNotes: Correct. Only the files brought into the last stage with COPY --from remain.
The layers of earlier stages are not included in the final image. The final image is built from the last FROM.
The final image is based on scratch in the last FROM, and go build runs only once, during the build.

question: In Kubernetes, which of the following is the smallest unit that is deployed and managed, grouping one or more containers that share the same IP address and volumes?
choices: Node
Service
Pod
explanation: A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes places and runs. The containers in it share a network namespace, so they can talk to each other over localhost and can use the same volumes. Usually one Pod holds one application container, and helper containers, for example for forwarding logs, are sometimes added to the same Pod. Pods are disposable and get a new IP address when recreated, so they are normally managed indirectly through a Deployment or similar. A node is a machine on which Pods run, and a Service is a stable endpoint for several Pods.
choiceNotes: A node is a physical or virtual machine that runs Pods. Many Pods run on one node.
A Service lets clients connect to several Pods selected by labels through a stable name and address.
Correct. The containers in a Pod share the network and volumes.

question: In Kubernetes, a Deployment with replicas: 3 is running three Pods. Which of the following correctly describes what happens when one of these Pods is deleted with kubectl delete pod?
choices: The Deployment's setting is also rewritten to replicas: 2, and two Pods keep running
A controller detects that the actual number has fallen below the specified 3 and creates one new Pod
The other two Pods of the Deployment are also deleted, and the whole Deployment stops
explanation: In Kubernetes, users declare a desired state such as "run three Pods", and controllers repeatedly observe the actual state and act to bring it closer to the declaration when they differ (reconciliation). Deleting one Pod makes the actual number 2, so the ReplicaSet controller creates a new Pod to return to 3. When a Pod is lost because a node fails, the same mechanism recreates it on another node. To really reduce the number of Pods, change the Deployment's replicas instead of deleting Pods.
choiceNotes: Deleting a Pod does not change the replicas declared in the Deployment. Pods are created to close the gap with the declaration.
Correct. The controller closes the gap between the declared state and the actual state.
Only the deleted Pod is affected. Unless the Deployment is deleted, the other Pods keep running.

question: In a Kubernetes Deployment, the container image in the Pod template is changed to a new version. Which of the following correctly describes what happens with the default update strategy (RollingUpdate)?
choices: A new ReplicaSet is created, and Pods of the new version are added while Pods of the old version are removed. The old ReplicaSet stays with 0 Pods for rollback
The container image inside the running Pods is replaced with the new version in place without recreating the Pods, so neither the Pods' IP addresses nor their names change
All Pods of the old version are deleted at once and then the Pods of the new version are created together, so the service stops temporarily during the update
explanation: When the Pod template changes, a Deployment creates a ReplicaSet for the new template and, while confirming that new Pods have become ready, gradually reduces the Pods of the old ReplicaSet. A certain number of Pods therefore keep handling requests during the update. The old ReplicaSet is kept with 0 Pods, so kubectl rollout undo can return to the previous version. The strategy that deletes all Pods first and then recreates them is Recreate, which is used only when specified explicitly.
choiceNotes: Correct. Pods are replaced gradually while switching ReplicaSets.
Container images are never swapped in place inside a Pod. New Pods are created, and their IP addresses change.
This is the behavior of the Recreate strategy. The default RollingUpdate replaces Pods gradually.

question: A Deployment with replicas: 10 has the rolling update settings maxSurge: 25% and maxUnavailable: 25%. Which of the following correctly gives the upper limit of the total number of Pods and the lower limit of the number of available Pods during an update?
choices: Upper limit 12, lower limit 8
Upper limit 13, lower limit 7
Upper limit 13, lower limit 8
explanation: When a percentage is converted into a number of Pods, maxSurge is rounded up and maxUnavailable is rounded down. 10 × 25% = 2.5, so maxSurge becomes 3 and maxUnavailable becomes 2. The upper limit of the total number of Pods is 10 + 3 = 13, and the lower limit of available Pods is 10 − 2 = 8. This rounding helps the update progress while ensuring that the number of available Pods never falls below the specified percentage.
choiceNotes: This rounds maxSurge's 2.5 down. maxSurge is rounded up to 3.
This rounds maxUnavailable's 2.5 up. maxUnavailable is rounded down to 2.
Correct. 10 + 3 = 13 and 10 − 2 = 8.

question: In Kubernetes, a Pod gets a different IP address every time it is recreated. Which of the following resources lets other applications connect, through a name and address that do not change, to several Pods selected by labels, with the load spread across them?
choices: ConfigMap
Service
PersistentVolume
explanation: A Service gives the set of Pods that match its label selector a virtual IP address and a DNS name that stay the same within the cluster, and distributes incoming traffic to those Pods. Even when Pods are replaced, clients only need to connect using the Service's name, so they do not need to know the Pods' addresses. To expose it outside the cluster, set the type to NodePort or LoadBalancer, or use an Ingress. A ConfigMap is a resource for configuration values, and a PersistentVolume is one for persistent storage.
choiceNotes: A ConfigMap is a resource for passing configuration values to Pods separately from the image.
Correct. A Service distributes traffic to several Pods through a stable name and address.
A PersistentVolume is a resource representing storage that remains even when Pods are recreated.

question: In a Kubernetes cluster, HTTPS requests arriving for one host name should be routed to the api Service if the path begins with /api, and to the web Service otherwise. Which of the following resources is suitable for defining this routing rule?
choices: Ingress
ReplicaSet
A Service of type: ClusterIP
explanation: An Ingress is a resource that defines rules for routing HTTP and HTTPS requests from outside the cluster to Services according to the host name and URL path, and TLS termination can also be configured there. The component that actually receives and routes the requests is an Ingress controller installed in the cluster (which acts as a reverse proxy). A Service of type: ClusterIP is an endpoint reachable only from inside the cluster and has no path-based routing. A ReplicaSet keeps the number of Pods and has nothing to do with routing traffic.
choiceNotes: Correct. It routes requests to Services by host name and path.
A ReplicaSet keeps the specified number of Pods running.
A ClusterIP Service is an endpoint inside the cluster and does not route by URL path.

question: A database password is stored in a Kubernetes Secret. Which of the following correctly describes a Secret?
choices: Values put in a Secret are automatically encrypted with strong cryptography, so no one in the cluster who reads them can learn the original password
Secret values cannot be referenced from containers, so the password has to be written in a configuration file inside the image
By default the values are merely represented in Base64, which is not encryption, so restricting who can read them and encryption at rest are used as well
explanation: A Secret is a resource for managing confidential values such as passwords and API keys separately from images and Pod definitions and passing them to containers as environment variables or files. However, the values written in a manifest are only represented in Base64, which anyone can decode. Also, by default, they are stored unencrypted in etcd, where the cluster's data is kept. Measures such as limiting with RBAC who can read Secrets and enabling encryption at rest for etcd are therefore used together.
choiceNotes: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Anyone with permission to read the value can decode it.
Secrets can be passed to containers as environment variables or files. A password written in the image becomes known to anyone who can pull the image.
Correct. Base64 is not encryption, so combine it with access restrictions and encryption at rest.

question: A web application cannot handle requests for about 60 seconds after starting, while it loads its cache, and returns 503 from /ready during that time. Which of the following correctly describes the effect of adding the settings above to the Pod's container?
choices: While /ready fails, the Pod is removed from the Service's routing targets and receives no requests, and the container is not restarted
The container is restarted each time /ready fails, so it keeps restarting before the cache has finished loading
Until /ready succeeds, the Pod is not assigned to any node, and the container is not started
explanation: A readiness probe checks whether a container is ready to accept requests and, while it fails, removes the Pod from the Service's routing targets. An HTTP probe treats a response of at least 200 and below 400 as success, so no requests are routed while 503 is returned, and requests arrive once the application is ready. Restarting the container on failure is the job of a liveness probe; giving an application that is slow to start only a liveness probe with a short interval can cause repeated restarts. Which node a Pod runs on is decided by the scheduler, not by probes.
choiceNotes: Correct. A readiness probe decides whether requests are routed to the Pod.
Restarting on failure is done by a liveness probe. A readiness probe failure does not restart the container.
Probes are run against containers that have already been assigned to a node and started. Assignment is decided by the scheduler.

question: In a web application on Kubernetes, the check performed by the liveness probe was made to include whether the application can connect to the database it depends on. Which of the following is the most likely problem with this setting?
choices: When the database stops, the Pods are automatically moved to the node where the database runs, degrading the other applications on that node
A brief database outage makes the containers of all Pods restart repeatedly, delaying recovery even after the database comes back
When the liveness probe fails, the Pod is only removed from the Service's routing targets, so no particular problem arises
explanation: A liveness probe exists to recover a container that has itself stopped responding (for example, through a deadlock) by restarting it. If it also checks a dependency, then when the database stops, the liveness probes of all Pods fail and the containers keep being restarted, even though restarting does not fix anything. During restarts no requests are handled, and the wait before the next restart may grow as restarts repeat, so recovery is delayed even after the database comes back. A liveness probe should check only whether the process itself can respond, and the state of dependencies should be handled by readiness probes or the application's error handling as needed.
choiceNotes: A probe failure never moves a Pod to another node. When a liveness probe fails, the container is restarted.
Correct. A failure of a dependency causes the Pods to be restarted again and again.
Removing a Pod from the routing targets is what a readiness probe does. When a liveness probe fails, the container is restarted.

question: A Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler has a target CPU utilization of 70% and a range of 1 to 10 Pods. Currently the average CPU utilization of 5 Pods is 30%. When the required number of Pods is computed as ⌈current number × current utilization ÷ target utilization⌉ (⌈ ⌉ means rounding up), which of the following is the required number of Pods?
explanation: A HorizontalPodAutoscaler determines the number of Pods as required number = ⌈current number × current utilization ÷ target utilization⌉. 5 × 30 ÷ 70 = 2.14…, which rounds up to 3. The same formula reduces the number when load falls (scale-in), and the result is kept within the specified range (1 to 10). In practice, a tolerance band leaves the number unchanged when the utilization ratio is close to 1, and a waiting period observes the load for a while before scaling in, so the number of Pods does not change too often.
choiceNotes: This rounds 2.14… down. With 2 Pods the utilization per Pod would be 30 × 5 ÷ 2 = 75%, above the 70% target, so the value is rounded up.
Correct. 5 × 30 ÷ 70 = 2.14…, rounded up to 3.
This swaps the target and current utilization (5 × 70 ÷ 30 = 11.7…, rounded up). The utilization is below the target, so the number of Pods goes down.

question: In a Deployment whose Pod containers have the settings above, four Pods are running, each using 400m (0.4 cores) of CPU. The HorizontalPodAutoscaler's target CPU utilization is 60%, and the required number of Pods is computed as ⌈current number × current utilization ÷ target utilization⌉. Which of the following is the required number of Pods?
explanation: The CPU utilization used by a HorizontalPodAutoscaler is a percentage of requests, not of limits. Each Pod uses 400m ÷ 500m = 80%, so the required number is 4 × 80 ÷ 60 = 5.33…, which rounds up to 6. With 6 Pods, the total usage of 400m × 4 = 1,600m is shared at about 267m each, a utilization of about 53%, below the target. If requests are not set, autoscaling based on CPU utilization does not work.
choiceNotes: This uses the 40% utilization relative to the limit (1000m) (4 × 40 ÷ 60 = 2.67…, rounded up). Utilization is based on requests.
This rounds 5.33… down. With 5 Pods each would use 1,600m ÷ 5 = 320m, a utilization of 64%, above the 60% target.
Correct. With 80% utilization, 4 × 80 ÷ 60 = 5.33… rounds up to 6.

question: In Kubernetes, which of the following correctly describes the resource requests and limits set for a container?
choices: Nodes are chosen using requests, a container whose memory exceeds its limit may be killed, and CPU is held to the limit
The scheduler places Pods so that the sum of limits fits within a node's resources, and a container whose CPU usage exceeds its request is killed
Requests are the maximum a container can use, and when usage exceeds the request, the container is killed at once, whether for memory or CPU
explanation: Requests are the amount of resources a container wants reserved, and the scheduler chooses the node for a Pod so that the sum of the requests of the Pods on a node does not exceed the node's allocatable resources. Limits are the upper bound on usage. CPU can be shared over time, so when a container tries to exceed its CPU limit its use is held back (throttling), and processing slows down. Memory is hard to take back, so a container that tries to use more than its memory limit may be killed as out of memory (OOMKilled).
choiceNotes: Correct. Placement uses requests, the cap is the limit, and exceeding it is handled differently for CPU and memory.
Placement decisions use requests, not limits. Also, heavy CPU use does not get a container killed; its use is held back.
Using more than the request is allowed; the cap is the limit. Exceeding the CPU limit leads to throttling, not to the container being killed.

question: A node has allocatable resources of 4 CPU cores and 8 GiB of memory. Each Pod's container has requests of 500m CPU and 1.5 GiB memory and limits of 1 CPU core and 2 GiB memory. There are no other Pods and no system reservations. Which of the following is the maximum number of Pods that can be placed on this node?
explanation: The scheduler places Pods so that the sum of the requests of the Pods on a node does not exceed the allocatable amount, for CPU and for memory separately. CPU allows up to 4000m ÷ 500m = 8 Pods, but memory allows 8 ÷ 1.5 = 5.33…, that is, up to 5. Both conditions must hold, so the answer is 5. Limits are not used for placement, so the limits of the 5 Pods add up to 5 CPU cores and 10 GiB of memory, more than the node has, and resources run short if all Pods use their maximum at the same time.
choiceNotes: This is the value computed from limits (CPU 4 ÷ 1 = 4, memory 8 ÷ 2 = 4). Placement is decided by requests.
Correct. CPU allows 8 Pods and memory 5, so the smaller number, 5, applies.
This uses only the CPU requests. The total memory requests must also fit within 8 GiB.

question: A managed database service in the cloud (one in which the provider operates the database software) is used. Under the shared responsibility model, which of the following generally remains the user's responsibility?
choices: Applying security fixes to the OS of the servers running the database and to the database software
Protecting the data center buildings and physical equipment such as servers from failures and intrusion
Managing the database user accounts and privileges, the network ranges allowed to connect, and the data stored
explanation: Under the shared responsibility model, the cloud provider and the user share the responsibility for security and operations, and where the boundary lies depends on the type of service. With a managed database service, the provider takes care not only of the physical facilities but also of updating the OS and the database software. On the other hand, who may access which data, which networks may connect and what data is stored remain the user's responsibility in every type of service. An accident in which a misconfiguration exposes a database to the internet is a problem on the user's side.
choiceNotes: In a managed service, updates to the OS and the database software are generally handled by the provider.
Managing physical facilities is the provider's responsibility in every type of service.
Correct. Access privileges, connection permissions and data management remain with the user.

question: In the cloud, which of the following is the main purpose of placing web servers and database replicas across several availability zones within the same region?
choices: To keep the service running in other zones even when a failure on the scale of a single data center (such as a power or cooling failure) occurs
To place servers in various parts of the world so that responses come from places near users, reducing communication latency
Because communication between zones has no latency and no charge, making processing faster and cheaper than in a single zone
explanation: A region is a geographic area where a cloud provider has data centers, and an availability zone within it is a group of one or more data centers whose power, cooling and networking are independent of the other zones. Zones are connected by low-latency links, so placing servers and data replicas across several zones lets the service continue in the remaining zones if one zone stops. To prepare for disasters that affect a whole area, replicas are also placed in another region. Communication between zones does have latency and may be charged, so the design must take the data replication method into account.
choiceNotes: Correct. Zones have independent power and networking, so the system can survive the failure of one zone.
Responding from places near users is the purpose of using several regions or a CDN. Zones in the same region are in nearby areas.
Communication between zones has latency and may be charged. The purpose is not speed or cost but preparing for failures.

question: With serverless functions (FaaS), only the first call to a function that has not been called for a while sometimes responds hundreds of milliseconds to several seconds slower. Which of the following correctly explains this phenomenon?
choices: The result of the first call is cached, and from the second call on the function code is not executed and only the stored result is returned
It takes time to prepare a new environment to run the function, start the language runtime and run initialization (a cold start)
On the first call the function code is sent to the user's device, compiled there and then executed
explanation: For serverless functions, the provider prepares execution environments (such as containers or lightweight virtual machines) as needed and cleans them up when they are not used for a while. The first call after an environment has been cleaned up requires preparing the environment, starting the language runtime and running the function's initialization, and the response is slower by that amount. Subsequent calls reuse the prepared environment and are faster (a warm start). Countermeasures include keeping initialization and the libraries loaded light and using settings that keep a certain number of environments ready in advance.
choiceNotes: Function results are not cached automatically; the code runs on every call.
Correct. The time to prepare and initialize the environment is added to the first call.
Functions run in execution environments on the cloud side. They are not sent to the user's device to run.

question: Cloud storage is used for three purposes: (1) attaching it to a virtual machine as a disk, creating a file system and storing database data files; (2) mounting it from several servers at the same time and using it as a shared directory; (3) reading and writing a large number of images by key (name) through an HTTP API and growing the capacity without deciding it in advance. Which of the following is the appropriate combination of storage types for (1) to (3)?
choices: (1) object storage, (2) block storage, (3) file storage
(1) file storage, (2) object storage, (3) block storage
(1) block storage, (2) file storage, (3) object storage
explanation: Block storage attaches an area of fixed size to a virtual machine as a virtual disk; a file system is created on it, and it suits uses such as databases that perform many small reads and writes quickly. File storage provides a shared file system that several servers can mount at the same time through NFS, SMB or the like. Object storage reads and writes data as whole objects identified by keys through an HTTP API; its capacity can be grown almost without limit, and it suits images, backups and logs. It is not suited to rewriting part of an object, so database data files are not placed in it.
choiceNotes: Object storage is not suited to fine-grained rewriting as a file system, and block storage is generally not used as a directory shared by several servers.
Object storage is not suited to a shared directory that is mounted, and block storage is not read and written through an HTTP API.
Correct. Disks are block storage, sharing is file storage, and large amounts of data handled through an API are object storage.

question: Virtual machines that are charged only for the time used, at ¥40 per hour (a made-up price), are used. Normally 2 machines run throughout the month (30 days), and on 20 weekdays 4 more are added for 6 hours a day to match the load. Which of the following is the charge for the month?
explanation: With pay-as-you-go pricing, the charge is number of machines × hours run × unit price. The 2 regular machines run 2 × 24 × 30 = 1,440 hours and the 4 added machines 4 × 6 × 20 = 480 hours, 1,920 hours in total. The charge is 1,920 × 40 = ¥76,800. Running 6 machines all the time to cover the peak would cost 6 × 720 × 40 = ¥172,800, so adjusting the number of machines to the load keeps the cost below half.
choiceNotes: This counts the 4 added machines on all 30 days instead of the 20 weekdays ((1,440 + 4 × 6 × 30) × 40 = ¥86,400).
This is the value for running 6 machines all month (6 × 720 × 40).

question: A virtual machine costs ¥50 per hour on demand, paying only for the hours used, or ¥262,800 per year with a reservation that commits to a year of use in advance, regardless of the hours used (both made-up prices). With a year taken as 8,760 hours, the reservation becomes cheaper once the hours used in a year exceed a certain number. Which of the following is that number of hours?
choices: 3,504 hours (40% of the year)
5,256 hours (60% of the year)
8,760 hours (100% of the year)
explanation: The reservation costs ¥262,800 regardless of the hours used, and on demand costs ¥50 × hours used, so the two are equal at 262,800 ÷ 50 = 5,256 hours. This is 5,256 ÷ 8,760 = 60%, so if the machine is used for more than 60% of the year, the reservation is cheaper. Converted to an hourly rate, the reservation is 262,800 ÷ 8,760 = ¥30, which is 40% cheaper than on demand. A common approach is to reserve servers that always run and use on demand for the extra capacity added to match the load.
choiceNotes: This confuses the reservation's discount rate (¥30 is 40% cheaper than ¥50) with the share of hours used.
Correct. 262,800 ÷ 50 = 5,256 hours, 60% of the year.
The reservation does not need year-round use to pay off. Above 5,256 hours, the reservation is cheaper.

question: Which of the following generally applies to how many public clouds charge for data transfer?
choices: Data transfer is free, and only the volume of stored data and the hours virtual machines run are charged
Transfer from the internet into the cloud is charged by volume, and transfer from the cloud out to anywhere else is free
Transfer in from the internet is free or cheap, and transfer out to the internet (egress) is charged by volume
explanation: In many clouds, transfer in the direction of bringing data in is free or cheap, and transfer out of the cloud is charged by volume. Transfer between availability zones or between regions may also be charged. For services that deliver large amounts of data, this transfer charge can exceed the compute charge, so the volume going out is reduced by design choices such as using CDN caches, compressing data and processing data close to where it is stored. Pricing differs between providers and services, so check it before designing.
choiceNotes: In many clouds, outbound transfer is charged and can become a large amount depending on the usage.
The directions are reversed. Generally, inbound transfer is free or cheap and outbound transfer is charged.
Correct. Designing to reduce outbound transfer leads to lower costs.

question: An environment was created by applying, with a declarative IaC (Infrastructure as Code) tool, a file that defines a network and two virtual machines. Immediately afterwards, the same file is applied again without any changes. Which of the following is what happens?
choices: There is no difference between the definition and the actual state, so nothing is changed
Another identical set is created, giving four virtual machines
Because the environment already exists, the second apply stops with an error
explanation: With declarative IaC, the code describes the desired configuration rather than the steps, and the tool compares it with the actual state and creates, changes or deletes only what differs. Applying the same definition any number of times therefore gives the same result (idempotence), and the second apply changes nothing. If someone changes a setting by hand and the actual state drifts from the definition (configuration drift), the next apply brings it back to the defined state. Managing the definitions in Git also allows history checks and reviews in the same way as for programs.
choiceNotes: Correct. Only the differences are changed, so applying the same definition any number of times leads to the same state.
This could happen if a script describing the creation steps were run twice. A declarative tool does not recreate what already exists.
A declarative tool compares existing resources with the definition and does nothing if there is no difference.

question: Which of the following is an appropriate way to update the software on production servers in line with the idea of immutable infrastructure?
choices: Log in to the running production servers with SSH, update the packages and then restart the service
Create new servers from a new image that includes the update, switch over to them, and discard the old servers without modifying them
Rewrite the configuration files by hand without stopping the production servers, and record the changes in a work log
explanation: With immutable infrastructure, servers (virtual machines or containers) are never modified once created; when a change is needed, new ones are created from an image that includes the change and swapped in. Because every server is created from the same image, configurations do not drift apart from server to server through accumulated manual differences. When a problem occurs, recreating from the previous image restores the old state. Anything that must be kept, such as logs and data, is stored in storage or databases outside the servers.
choiceNotes: This modifies running servers directly and causes the state of each server to drift.
Correct. Changes go into the image, and whole servers are replaced.
Even with a record, the running servers are still changed by hand, which is not the immutable approach.

question: Two environments with the same configuration as production are prepared; the current version keeps running in one while the new version is installed and checked in the other, and then the load balancer is switched over to it all at once. If there is a problem, switching back quickly returns to the old version. Which of the following is this release method?
choices: Blue-green deployment
Canary release
Rolling update
explanation: Blue-green deployment prepares two environments (blue and green) and switches user traffic to the new environment all at once. The old environment is left as it is for a while, so if a problem occurs, simply switching back restores the old version. On the other hand, resources for two environments are needed around the switch, and database schema changes must be made in a form that both the old and new versions can use. A canary release exposes the new version to only some of the requests, and a rolling update replaces servers a few at a time.
choiceNotes: Correct. Two environments are prepared, and traffic is switched all at once.
A canary release first sends only some requests to the new version and increases the share while watching how it behaves.
A rolling update replaces the servers or Pods in one environment with the new version a few at a time.

question: A service that receives 12,000 requests per hour performs a canary release of a new version, sending only 5% of the requests to it. The new version has a bug that makes 3% of the requests it receives fail; it is noticed after one hour, and all requests are returned to the old version. Which of the following is the number of requests that failed because of the bug during that hour?
explanation: The new version received 12,000 × 5% = 600 requests, and 3% of them failed, so 600 × 3% = 18 requests failed. Had all requests been switched to the new version at once, 12,000 × 3% = 360 would have failed. A canary release limits the requests affected by a bug to a small share in this way and increases the share if there is no problem, while watching indicators such as error rate and response time. Comparing the indicators of the new and old versions needs enough requests, so the share and the observation time are decided together.
choiceNotes: This is the number if all requests had been sent to the new version (12,000 × 0.03).
This is the number of requests sent to the new version (12,000 × 0.05); only 3% of them failed.

question: A container image built by a CI/CD pipeline was tested in the staging environment and passed. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to release this image to production?
choices: Build the image again from the same source code for production and release that to production
Retag the tested image as latest, and pull latest in the production environment
Release the tested image itself to production by specifying its digest, and supply the differences between environments through configuration
explanation: In a pipeline, the artifact produced by the build (here, the image) is treated as unchangeable, and the same artifact is promoted from staging to production. Even from the same source code, a rebuild may pick up different versions of the libraries or base image it depends on, so something different from what was tested would reach production. A tag can later be moved to another image, so to be sure of pointing to the same image, use the digest, which is determined by the contents. Differences between environments, such as connection targets, are not built into the image but supplied through configuration such as environment variables.
choiceNotes: A rebuild may change dependent libraries and produce an image different from the one tested.
latest is a tag that can be moved, so at pull time it may point to a different image.
Correct. The digest guarantees that the same image that was tested goes to production.

question: As shown above, the database connection target is not written into the image but passed as an environment variable when the container starts. Which of the following is the most appropriate main advantage of this design?
code:
$ docker run -d -e DB_HOST=db.staging.example.com web:1.4.2
$ docker run -d -e DB_HOST=db.prod.example.com web:1.4.2
choices: Values put in environment variables are encrypted automatically, so even a password cannot be read by others
The same image can be used in staging and production, with only the settings changed and no rebuild, so what was tested can be released to production as is
The connection information does not go into the image's layers, so the image has fewer layers and containers start much faster
explanation: Passing configuration through environment variables is also recommended by the methodology called The Twelve-Factor App, and it separates the code and the image from the environment that runs them. The same image can be used in staging and production, so what reaches production is the same thing that was tested, and there is no need to rebuild the image each time the connection target changes. However, environment variables are not encrypted, so anyone who can see the container configuration or process information can read them. Confidential values such as passwords are passed through mechanisms such as Kubernetes Secrets that restrict who can read them.
choiceNotes: Environment variables are not encrypted. Anyone who can inspect the container configuration can read the values.
Correct. Differences between environments are moved into configuration, so the same image can be reused.
A few dozen bytes of settings make almost no difference to the number of layers or the start-up time. The main advantage is separating the image from the environment.

question: In a system in which several services work together, you want to find out which services a single user request passed through, in what order, and how much time it spent in each. Among the data used for observability, which of the following is the most suitable?
choices: Metrics (numeric time series such as CPU utilization and request counts)
Logs (records of events output by each service)
Traces (records of the path of one request and the time of each segment)
explanation: Observability is the degree to which the internal state of a system can be inferred from the data it emits, and metrics, logs and traces are often named as the data for it. In tracing (distributed tracing), an identifier shared by the request is passed between services, and the start and end times of the processing segments (spans) in each service are recorded to reconstruct the path of one request and the breakdown of its time. Metrics suit detecting overall trends and anomalies, and logs suit detailed investigation of individual events, but traces are the most suitable for following the flow of one request across services. In practice, the trace identifier is also written into the logs, and the three are combined to find causes.
choiceNotes: Metrics are aggregated numeric time series, suited to seeing overall trends and anomalies, but they do not show the path of one request.
Logs are records of individual events, separate for each service, so on their own they make it hard to connect the flow of one request.
Correct. A trace records the path and time of one request as it passes across services.
